💬 Panama vs. England: Injuries, predicted lineup & how to watch

📌 Panama vs. England match preview: Predicted lineup, injury news, and how to watch as the Three Lions aim to clinch Group L at the World Cup.

England aim to secure top spot in Group L when they face an already-eliminated Panama at MetLife Stadium. After a frustrating goalless draw against Ghana, Thomas Tuchel’s side needs to rediscover their attacking magic and urgency to break down a stubborn defensive block. With injuries mounting at the back and a place in the knockout rounds practically guaranteed, the Three Lions must find solutions on the right flank to head into the Round of 32 with winning momentum.
​
Thomas Tuchel is facing a major injury crisis at right-back. Reece James is ruled out with a minor hamstring problem, joining Tino Livramento, who was sent home with a calf injury. Midfielder Elliot Anderson is a major doubt due to muscle soreness and a glute issue. Declan Rice is also managing a calf issue and may be rested, as he is just one booking away from a suspension. Bukayo Saka, Marcus Rashford, and Morgan Rogers are all pushing to enter the starting eleven.
​
Already eliminated from the tournament after two defeats, Panama are dealing with internal friction ahead of their final group stage match. Cecilio Waterman and Jose Luis Rodriguez were involved in a training ground bust-up that required teammates to intervene. On the injury front, manager Thomas Christiansen will hope influential midfielder Adalberto Carrasquilla is fit to feature after being an unused substitute against Croatia.
​
Thomas Tuchel on the injury to Reece James: “He has a minor hamstring injury and is in an accelerated rehabilitation programme. I strongly believe he will be available for us in the tournament.”
​
When asked about James returning for the Round of 32, Tuchel added context: “It can be a tight one, but hopes are still alive.”
​
Tuchel on managing his depleted defense: He insisted he would “find solutions,” noting that Jarell Quansah has been “freed up” to play full-back following the call-up of Trevoh Chalobah.
​
Panama have suffered narrow back-to-back defeats in their opening World Cup matches.
​
England remain unbeaten but looked predictable and lacked urgency in their recent goalless draw.
​
The only previous meeting between these two nations resulted in a dominant six-goal display for the Three Lions.
​
England enter this fixture heavily favored to take all three points and cement their status as Group L winners. Despite Thomas Tuchel’s mounting injury headache at right-back, the Three Lions possess superior depth and quality across the pitch. After a sluggish and predictable performance against Ghana, England’s attacking stars—including potentially fresh faces like Marcus Rashford and Bukayo Saka—will be eager to inject urgency and put on a show at MetLife Stadium.
​
Panama, while much evolved since their 6-1 drubbing by England in 2018, come into this match with nothing to play for but pride. Training ground disruptions and consecutive scoreless defeats suggest a team struggling to find rhythm. If England can effectively dismantle Panama’s expected low block with quick passing and movement, they should secure a comfortable victory to carry momentum into the Round of 32.

Euro Digital: Europe is preparing money that will work even without the internet

Euro digital has taken a new step forward in Brussels.

The idea is for any citizen to be able to pay with a digital version of the euro, issued by the European Central Bank (ECB), including without an internet connection.

Payments can be made with a phone, card, online, and offline - and rely less on Visa, Mastercard, and private banks.

### What is already raising questions:
- Limits will be set on how much digital euros can be stored.
- Many stores may be required to accept it.
- Banks fear that some of the money will be taken from their accounts.
- Millions of citizens are concerned about privacy of data.

The ECB promises that digital euro will not replace cash, and offline payments will have an increased level of confidentiality (similar to cash).

However, the discussion in Europe has long gone beyond just the technology.

This is a question of power: do we need public digital money or are we opening the door to too much control over how we pay?

📌 Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): Portable IDs for Web3

Main Points
⏺ DIDs are identifiers you control, not usernames owned by platforms
⏺ They can link to verifiable credentials like diplomas or KYC checks
⏺ This post explains how DIDs help build portable identity across apps

1️⃣ What Is a DID — a standardized identifier tied to keys you own, not to an email, phone number, or single company.
2️⃣ Verifiable Credentials — organizations can sign claims about you (for example, “passed KYC”, “finished course”) that you can present elsewhere.
3️⃣ User Control — you decide when and where to share proofs instead of giving every app full personal data.
4️⃣ Interoperability — multiple dApps, wallets, and even Web2 services can recognize the same DID as “you”.
5️⃣ Privacy Angle — combined with zero-knowledge proofs, DIDs can prove facts (age, residency, reputation) without revealing raw documents.

Final Thoughts

Decentralized identifiers turn identity from siloed accounts into something you own and reuse — a core building block for Web3 logins and reputation.

Former Ethereum Foundation developer Trent Van Epps warns that Ethereum could face a funding crisis within the next 3–9 months 

For years, the Ethereum Foundation has followed a “subtraction” strategy—gradually reducing its influence so the network can thrive independently. However, EF still remains a key pillar of legitimacy through its brand, ties to Vitalik Buterin, developer events, and ecosystem coordination.

The bigger issue is funding. After spending much of its ETH reserves on ecosystem growth, EF plans to cut annual spending from 15% to 5% by 2030. Meanwhile, its 4-year Client Incentive Program ended in April 2026 with no replacement announced.

Maintaining client teams, research, and protocol coordination costs around $30M per year. Without a sustainable funding model, Ethereum risks losing experienced developers and slowing progress on scaling, quantum-resistance research, and core network maintenance.

Ethereum’s biggest challenge may not be technology—it may be funding the people building it.
